finding.lifecycle.dialogPresent.name: Dialog still present
finding.lifecycle.dialogPresent.why: Dialogs were removed in 2020. One sitting here means nobody has audited this solution in five years, which is worth knowing before reading any other number in this report.
finding.lifecycle.dialogPresent.recommen: Delete it. If the process it described still matters, it is being done by hand now and nobody has noticed.
finding.lifecycle.deprecatedClientApi.na: Deprecated client API in a web resource
finding.lifecycle.deprecatedClientApi.wh: Removed client APIs fail at run time, on a form, in front of a user, with no build to catch it first.
finding.lifecycle.deprecatedClientApi.re: Replace each call with its documented successor. The checker names the replacement.
finding.lifecycle.classicWorkflowInUse.w: Not deprecated, and the designer has had no investment in years. The cost is that the people who can maintain it are becoming the people who remember it.
finding.lifecycle.classicWorkflowInUse.r: Replace when you are in the component for another reason. A migration project of its own is rarely worth funding on this finding alone, and a report that says otherwise is overselling.
finding.lifecycle.classicWorkflowDormant: Classic workflow activated and never running
Either it is dead and should go, or it should have run and did not, which is worse.
Confirm which of the two it is before deleting anything.
finding.lifecycle.customWorkflowActivity: Custom workflow activity pinning a classic workflow
The workflow cannot be replaced until the code has somewhere to go, so this is the finding that sets the order of the modernisation backlog.
Move the logic to a custom API or a plugin first, then replace the workflow.
finding.lifecycle.rdlReport.name: RDL report
finding.lifecycle.rdlReport.why: Supported, static, and where reporting stopped. Each one is a Power BI candidate with a real hours cost, which is why they are listed individually rather than summarised.
finding.lifecycle.rdlReport.recommendati: Inventory, then decide per report. A report nobody has run in a year is a deletion, not a migration.
finding.lifecycle.dataflowPresent.name: Dataflow in the estate
finding.lifecycle.dataflowPresent.why: No CLI support and no catalogue API, so a dataflow does not travel through an ALM pipeline and does not appear in most governance tooling. It also consumes Dataverse capacity in a way that surfaces as a bill rather than as an alert.
finding.lifecycle.dataflowPresent.recomm: Decide whether it is load bearing. If it is, rebuild it somewhere that can be versioned.
finding.architecture.logicSpread.name: One table with logic in more than three places
finding.architecture.logicSpread.why: This is the finding that explains why a change on that table takes three weeks and breaks something unrelated. Nobody can hold the order of execution in their head, and no document describes it.
finding.architecture.logicSpread.recomme: Map what fires on create and on update, in order, and consolidate. The map is most of the value even if nothing is consolidated.
finding.architecture.proCodeWhereConfigW: Script doing what a business rule does
Code that has to be deployed to do something configuration does, which means a maker has to raise a ticket to change a field label's behaviour.
Replace with a business rule, entity scoped if the same validation needs to hold server side.
finding.architecture.lowCodeRatio.name: Low code to high code ratio
finding.architecture.lowCodeRatio.why: A number the client asked for, which means it will be quoted without its definition. The definition travels with it in every export for that reason.
finding.architecture.lowCodeRatio.recomm: Read it next to the domain breakdown. A high pro code share in the integration domain is normal. The same share in the logic domain is a finding.
finding.architecture.externalLogicInvisi: Logic outside the platform with no documented owner
A solution can look clean while most of its behaviour sits in an Azure Function nobody in the room has seen. This finding puts a floor under how much of that there is.
Name an owner and a repository for each one. The report cannot tell you what is behind the URL.
finding.quality.flowNoErrorHandling.name: Cloud flow with no failure path
finding.quality.flowNoErrorHandling.why: It fails silently. The run history knows, and the run history is not something anybody reads unprompted.
finding.quality.flowNoErrorHandling.reco: Wrap the body in a scope with a configure run after handler that reports the failure somewhere a person looks.
finding.quality.flowFailureRate.name: Cloud flow failing regularly
finding.quality.flowFailureRate.why: Something is broken now. Whether anybody has noticed is a separate question and usually has the same answer.
finding.quality.flowFailureRate.recommen: Read the last failure before estimating anything. A flow failing on a data condition is a different job from one failing on an expired connection.
finding.quality.flowSize.name: Cloud flow too large to reason about
finding.quality.flowSize.why: Low code by construction and unmaintainable in practice. Nobody changes one of these confidently, so eventually nobody changes it at all.
finding.quality.flowSize.recommendation: Split into child flows along the steps a person would describe out loud.
finding.quality.canvasDelegationWarnings: It works in test with two hundred rows and returns wrong answers in production with fifty thousand. Wrong answers, not slow ones, which is why this is high rather than medium.
Fix the ones over a table with real volume first. A delegation warning over a lookup table of twelve rows is noise.
finding.quality.pluginNoTracing.name: Plugin with no tracing
finding.quality.pluginNoTracing.why: When it throws in production there is nothing to read.
finding.quality.pluginNoTracing.recommen: Add tracing at the entry and exit of each handler and at every branch that can throw.
finding.quality.pluginNotSandboxed.name: Plugin assembly not in sandbox isolation
finding.quality.pluginNotSandboxed.why: It cannot be deployed to an online environment and it cannot be moved. This is usually a finding about where the solution came from rather than about the code.
finding.quality.pluginNotSandboxed.recom: Rebuild against sandbox isolation. Expect to find something in there that needs full trust and to have a longer conversation about it.
finding.quality.formScriptOnLoadWeight.n: Form loading more script than it needs
finding.quality.formScriptOnLoadWeight.w: Form load time is the thing users complain about and the thing nobody measures.
finding.quality.formScriptOnLoadWeight.r: Register libraries where they are used rather than everywhere, and check whether the large one is a framework that could be a platform library instead.
finding.alm.unmanagedInProduction.name: Unmanaged customisation in a production environment
finding.alm.unmanagedInProduction.why: There is no pipeline. Whatever is here was made here, and the environment is the source of truth, which means there is no rollback and no review.
finding.alm.unmanagedInProduction.recomm: This is not a component finding. It is a delivery finding and it outranks everything else in the report.
finding.alm.defaultSolutionComponents.na: Components living in the default solution
finding.alm.defaultSolutionComponents.wh: They do not travel. Somebody will find out when the next deployment is missing a column.
finding.alm.defaultSolutionComponents.re: Move each one into a named solution with a publisher prefix that means something.
finding.alm.publisherPrefixSprawl.name: More than one publisher prefix in one solution
finding.alm.publisherPrefixSprawl.why: Usually means two teams, or one team and a consultancy, building in the same place without agreeing anything. Harmless on its own and a reliable signal of something else.
finding.alm.publisherPrefixSprawl.recomm: Leave existing components alone. Renaming a prefix is not a thing you can do. Agree the prefix for new work.
finding.alm.missingConnectionReference.n: Flow with an embedded connection rather than a reference
finding.alm.missingConnectionReference.w: It will import and it will not run, and the error will be reported by whoever tested the wrong thing first.
finding.alm.missingConnectionReference.r: Add a connection reference per connector and repoint the flow.
finding.alm.hardCodedEnvironmentValue.wh: The solution imports cleanly into test and points at production.
finding.alm.hardCodedEnvironmentValue.re: Replace with an environment variable. Leave the default value empty rather than setting it to the development value.
finding.alm.environmentVariableWithDefau: Environment variable shipping a default value
The default travels into the target environment and looks like a deliberate setting. Nobody changes it because nothing says it needs changing.
Ship the definition, set the value per environment in the pipeline.
finding.governance.orphanedColumn.name: Column on no form and no view
finding.governance.orphanedColumn.why: The most common finding in this product by volume, and the one to be most careful with. A column with no interface reference is often written by an integration.
finding.governance.orphanedColumn.recomm: Check the API usage before proposing a deletion. Report the count prominently and the individual deletions cautiously.
finding.governance.securityRoleSprawl.wh: Every one of these is a decision somebody made and nobody recorded. They also make the role picker unusable, which is how people end up assigning System Administrator.
finding.governance.securityRoleSprawl.re: Delete, after checking it is not assigned by a provisioning process that runs monthly.
Custom role with organisation level write
Usually granted to make something work during a go live and never narrowed afterwards.
Narrow to business unit or user level and test what breaks. Something will.
finding.security.secretInDefinition.name: Secret in a component definition
finding.security.secretInDefinition.why: It is in the solution file, which means it is in source control, which means rotating it is the smallest part of the job.
finding.security.secretInDefinition.reco: Rotate first, then move to Key Vault through an environment variable. In that order.
finding.governance.premiumConnectorExpos: A licensing conversation, not a technical one. Reported as information because this product cannot see what licences the tenant holds and should not guess.
Check the finding against the licences in place before drawing a conclusion.
finding.governance.orphanedByOwner.name: Component owned by a disabled user
finding.governance.orphanedByOwner.why: A flow owned by somebody who left runs on their connections until those expire, and then it stops, and nobody knows why.
finding.governance.orphanedByOwner.recom: Reassign to a service principal or a group owned solution. Reassigning to another person recreates the problem with a later date on it.
finding.performance.plugSyncSlow.name: Synchronous plugin running long
finding.performance.plugSyncSlow.why: It is inside the user's save. Everything above two seconds is felt.
finding.performance.plugSyncSlow.recomme: Move what does not need to be in the transaction out of it.
finding.performance.stepNoFilteringAttri: Update step with no filtering attributes
It runs on every change to every column on that table, including the ones written by other plugins, which is also how recursion starts.
List the columns the handler actually reads.
finding.performance.viewComplexity.name: View joining too much
finding.performance.viewComplexity.why: It is the first thing every user of that table loads.
finding.performance.viewComplexity.recom: Trim the default view. Keep the wide one as a named alternative.
finding.operability.noFailureAlerting.na: No failure alerting anywhere in the solution
finding.operability.noFailureAlerting.wh: Everything above about failure rates assumes somebody finds out. This rule checks that assumption once, at the solution level, rather than repeating it per component.
finding.operability.noFailureAlerting.re: One failure path that reaches a person beats per component handling that reaches a run history.
finding.operability.noEnvironmentSeparat: Same components present in every environment as unmanaged
There is no promotion path, there is copying. The versions have already diverged, which is why the finding is critical rather than high.
Pick the environment that is closest to right and make it the source. This is a project rather than a fix.
finding.quality.namingInconsistent.name: Inconsistent naming across a solution
finding.quality.namingInconsistent.why: Cosmetic, cheap to report and consistently the thing a client points at first in a workshop. It is also a proxy for how many people have built here without a standard.
finding.quality.namingInconsistent.recom: Agree a convention for new work. Renaming existing components is rarely worth the regression risk.
finding.quality.missingDescription.name: Component with no description
finding.quality.missingDescription.why: The cost lands on whoever inherits this, which on a consultancy engagement is the client.
finding.quality.missingDescription.recom: Fill in descriptions as part of whatever work touches the component. A separate description backlog never gets done.
finding.performance.pcfBundleSize.name: Code component with a heavy bundle
finding.performance.pcfBundleSize.why: The bundle is downloaded before the field appears. It is paid on every form load, by every user.
finding.performance.pcfBundleSize.recomm: Look at what is inside it. Usually a library included whole for one function.
finding.modernisation.pcfBundlesOwnReact: Code component shipping its own React
A virtual control borrows the host's React instead of bundling a second copy onto the form.
Convert it to a virtual control. Worth doing where the bundle is large or several controls share a form.
finding.quality.pcfNotMinified.name: Code component shipped unminified
finding.quality.pcfNotMinified.why: It was built in development configuration and deployed that way.
finding.quality.pcfNotMinified.recommend: Ship a production build. If nobody knows which build is running, that is the finding.
finding.quality.pcfDebugCodeShipped.name: Debug code left in a code component
finding.quality.pcfDebugCodeShipped.why: A debugger statement stops the browser of anybody who has developer tools open.
finding.quality.pcfDebugCodeShipped.reco: Strip it in the production build rather than by hand.
finding.performance.pcfPollingTimer.name: Code component polling on a timer
finding.performance.pcfPollingTimer.why: The timer runs for as long as the form stays open, for every user at once. It is the one cost that does not end when the page finishes loading.
finding.performance.pcfPollingTimer.reco: Check what it does and that it is cleared in destroy. A control showing elapsed time needs one; a control polling for changes usually does not.
finding.security.pcfInnerHtml.name: Code component writing HTML directly
finding.security.pcfInnerHtml.why: Whatever reaches that assignment is parsed as markup. Where it comes from a record, a user decides what runs.
finding.security.pcfInnerHtml.recommenda: Check where the strings come from. Anything built from record data wants textContent. Constant markup is fine.
finding.quality.pcfUndeclaredWebApi.name: Code component using the Web API without declaring it
finding.quality.pcfUndeclaredWebApi.why: The platform only hands over the features the manifest asked for. It fails at the first call, not at form load.
finding.quality.pcfUndeclaredWebApi.reco: Add the feature usage to the manifest and rebuild. One line.
finding.ai.agentGenerativeNoGrounding.na: Agent answering generatively with nothing to answer from
finding.ai.agentGenerativeNoGrounding.wh: Generative answers with no knowledge source means the model answers from what it already knows, to a customer, in the organisation's name. The failure is not an error message: it is a confident and plausible answer nobody can trace to a source.
finding.ai.agentGenerativeNoGrounding.re: Either attach the knowledge the agent is meant to answer from, or turn generative answers off and let the topics handle it. Both are defensible; the combination of the two settings is not.
finding.ai.agentNoTopics.name: Agent with no deterministic topics
finding.ai.agentNoTopics.why: Every answer is then generated, including the ones with a right answer. A topic is the only part of an agent somebody can point at and say what it will do.
finding.ai.agentNoTopics.recommendation: Author topics for the questions that have one correct answer, and let the model handle the long tail.
finding.ai.agentUnpublished.name: Agent built and never published
finding.ai.agentUnpublished.why: It cost somebody the time to build and it answers nobody. Either it was abandoned, or it was forgotten before go live.
finding.ai.agentUnpublished.recommendati: Publish it or delete it. An agent in neither state is a decision nobody has made.
finding.ai.modelStale.name: AI Builder model not retrained in a year
finding.ai.modelStale.why: A prediction model is a statement about data as it was when the model was trained. The data moves, the model does not, and it keeps answering with the same confidence it had on the day it was trained.
finding.ai.modelStale.recommendation: Retrain it against current data and compare the scores. Where nobody can say what the model is used for any more, unpublish it and find out.
finding.ai.modelUnpublished.name: AI Builder model trained and never published
finding.ai.modelUnpublished.why: Training consumed credits and produced something nothing can call.
finding.ai.modelUnpublished.recommendati: Publish it where something is waiting for it, delete it where nothing is.
finding.ai.realtimeVoiceInUse.name: Agent using realtime voice
finding.ai.realtimeVoiceInUse.why: A cost and licensing fact rather than a fault. Voice is metered differently from text and this product cannot see what the tenant is paying.
finding.ai.realtimeVoiceInUse.recommenda: Read it against the licences in place before drawing any conclusion from it.
finding.ai.agentOpenToAnyone.name: Published agent anyone can talk to
finding.ai.agentOpenToAnyone.why: Anybody who finds the address can talk to it, and it answers in the organisation's name. That is legitimate for a public help agent and serious for anything else, and the setting is the same either way.
finding.ai.agentOpenToAnyone.recommendat: Where the agent is meant to be public, record that it is and check what it is grounded in, because everything it says is public too. Where it is not, set authentication to integrated or restrict the access policy to a group.
finding.quality.descriptionUninformative: A description reading “test”, “tbd” or the name again costs the same to maintain as a good one and buys nothing. Empty descriptions are already reported, so the cheapest way to clear that finding is to type a character; this is what catches that.
Say what the component is for and what would break without it. One sentence is enough, and it is worth more than the name repeated.
finding.contactCenter.queueNoMembers.nam: Routing queue with nobody in it
finding.contactCenter.queueNoMembers.why: Work routed here is never offered to anybody. The customer waits until they give up, and nothing in the configuration looks wrong: the workstream is valid, the routing rule matches and the queue exists. It is the one fault that is invisible from every screen except this one.
finding.contactCenter.queueNoMembers.rec: Add the agents who should take this work, or remove the routing that sends work here. If the queue is a deliberate holding area, make that explicit with an overflow action rather than leaving work to wait for people who are never coming.
Work reaches the queue and stops there. Agents can pick it if they go and look, but nothing offers it to anybody, so on a push channel it waits exactly as long as it would in a queue with no members, while the queue itself shows a healthy membership.

Choose an assignment method, usually highest capacity or round robin. Keep No Assignment only for a queue that is meant to be worked by hand, and then make sure the workstreams feeding it are pick rather than push.
finding.contactCenter.capacityProfileUnh: Work from those workstreams needs an agent with this profile, and there is none, so no agent is ever eligible for it. It sits in the queue with every other setting correct, which makes it the most expensive contact centre fault to find from the outside.
Assign the profile to the agents who should take this work, or remove it from the workstreams that require it. Check the queue for work that has been waiting since the profile was added.
finding.contactCenter.workstreamNoDefaul: Work that matches none of the routing rules has nowhere to land. Every route can be correct today and the first conversation that falls between them disappears from the operation, usually on the day a new product launches and the rules have not caught up.
Set a default queue staffed by people who can triage anything, and watch its volume: work arriving there is a route that is missing.
finding.contactCenter.queueNoOverflow.wh: When the queue is full, out of hours or waiting too long, nothing happens: the work waits. Overflow is how a contact centre says what should happen instead -- another queue, a callback, a message -- and a queue without it has made that decision by default, in the customer’s time.
finding.contactCenter.queueNoOverflow.re: Decide what should happen when this queue cannot keep up, and configure it: transfer to a queue that can, offer a callback, or end the conversation with a message that says when to try again.
finding.contactCenter.queueNoOperatingHo: The queue is open every hour of every day as far as routing is concerned, so work arrives at three in the morning and waits for people who will not be there until nine. Customers are not told the line is closed; they are left in a queue.
Attach the operating hours the team actually keeps, and pair them with an overflow action for out-of-hours work so customers are told rather than kept waiting.
finding.contactCenter.queueNoServiceLeve: Service level reporting for this queue measures against nothing, so the figure a supervisor reads is not a figure about this queue. Nothing breaks; the numbers just stop meaning anything.
Set the threshold the business has actually agreed for this queue, in seconds.
finding.contactCenter.capacityProfileDai: Capacity profile that blocks for the rest of the day

An agent who reaches the maximum is offered nothing more from it until the next day. That is a legitimate cap -- twenty cases a day, say -- and a surprising one when it was meant to be a concurrency limit, because it looks the same in the form either way.
Confirm the daily cap is intended. If it was meant to limit how many items an agent holds at once, set the reset to immediate.
